strengths: The problem — assisting authors during the rebuttal phase with verifiable, evidence-linked responses rather than free-form generation — is relevant, timely, and underexplored relative to the growing literature on LLM-assisted peer review.

The system design is well-motivated: decomposing reviews into atomic concerns, constructing concern-conditioned hybrid contexts, on-demand external evidence retrieval, and a plan-before-drafting workflow with human checkpoints is a sensible instantiation of the 'verify-then-write' framing.

The paper provides an extensive set of prompts and rubric anchors in the appendix, improving transparency and reproducibility of the pipeline, and the benchmark is derived from a public source (Re²/ICLR 2023 OpenReview threads).

The evaluation covers multiple closed-source backbones with matched backbones between baseline and system, plus component ablations (input structuring, evidence construction, checkers), which is the right experimental structure in principle.
Case studies in Appendix E illustrate concrete qualitative differences (explicit action items, placeholder discipline) between the proposed system and direct generation baselines.
weaknesses: Critical internal contradiction on the paper's core claim of 'strict faithfulness': the Rebuttal Letter Writer prompt (Appendix D) MANDATES the model to 'invent plausible, realistic values/results' for missing experiments (marked with asterisks). This directly conflicts with the paper's central claims of 'no hallucination' and 'strict faithfulness to the submitted manuscript.' Worse, the LLM judge's A2 Evidence Support dimension explicitly rewards 'new quantitative results,' so fabricated numbers likely inflate the system's main scores. This undermines the validity of the central results.

The evaluation relies entirely on a single LLM judge (Gemini-3-Flash) that is itself one of the evaluated backbones, with no human evaluation and no validation of judge reliability. The paper has access to a natural validation signal (positive/negative reviewer follow-up outcomes) but never reports whether judge scores correlate with real post-rebuttal outcomes. Self-preference bias toward structured, evidence-linked output in the style of the rubric is a plausible confound.

The evaluation scale is very small: RebuttalBench-Challenge appears to contain only ~20 papers, and reported gains (0.3–0.5 on a 0–5 scale) come with no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Given LLM-judge noise, these margins may not be meaningful.

Baseline comparisons are not compute/cost-matched: RebuttalAgent uses many agent calls plus external search while baselines use single-pass prompting; the observed advantage could partly reflect more computation and retrieval rather than the structured workflow.

The dataset construction (LLM-based sentiment classification with confidence thresholds for positive/negative labels) is loosely specified and its reliability is unvalidated; the corpus-level vs. challenge-level split rationale is thin.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or data released at submission time, empty 'Project Page' and 'HF Demo' links, and no token/cost logging reported despite the appendix claiming outputs are logged.

Presentation sloppiness undermines confidence: the conclusion names the system 'RESPONSEAGENT' instead of RebuttalAgent, model names are inconsistent (GPT5-mini vs. GPT-5-mini), the citation for Gemini-3-Flash is dated 2023, and the 'final weighted score' is actually a simple average.

Novelty is moderate: the components (concern decomposition, retrieval augmentation, plan-then-draft, multi-agent orchestration) are established techniques applied to rebuttal writing; the contribution rests mainly on the application, benchmark, and empirical findings, which as noted above have validity issues.

strengths: The problem is relevant and well-motivated: rebuttal writing is a genuine, under-explored stage of the peer-review lifecycle, and the framing around coverage, faithfulness, verifiable grounding, and global consistency is sensible.

The pipeline design (concern decomposition, concern-conditioned hybrid context, on-demand external evidence with anti-fabrication guardrails in the retrieval prompts, plan verification before drafting) is clearly described, and the idea of inspectable intermediate artifacts with human checkpoints has practical value.
The paper provides full prompt templates for all agents and the judge in the appendix, which supports reproducibility of the system design.

The ablation study (input structuring, evidence construction, checkers) across multiple matched backbones is a useful design, and the matched-backbone comparison is a fair way to isolate the contribution of the workflow from model capacity.
Building a corpus of review-rebuttal-reaction threads with outcome-based labels (whether concerns were resolved) from public OpenReview data is a potentially useful resource.
weaknesses: Evaluation validity is the central weakness: all results rely on a single LLM judge (Gemini-3-Flash), with no human evaluation, no validation that the judge's scores correlate with expert or reviewer judgment, and no inter-annotator checks. This is especially problematic because the judge may systematically favor the structured, point-by-point, verbose output format that the proposed system is explicitly instructed to produce — the measured gains may largely reflect format/rubric gaming rather than genuine rebuttal quality.

There is circularity between benchmark, rubric, and system: the authors design the rubric from their own analysis, build the benchmark, build the system to satisfy that rubric, and then evaluate with an LLM judge using that rubric. No external validity signal (e.g., actual reviewer follow-up scores, acceptance outcomes) is used to validate the metric, despite the dataset containing such signals.

A serious soundness and ethics concern: the 'Rebuttal Letter Writer' prompt in Appendix D explicitly instructs the model to 'invent plausible, realistic values/results' for missing experiments, marking them with asterisks. This directly contradicts the paper's central claim of strict faithfulness and preventing hallucination/over-promising, and it normalizes fabricating empirical results in a high-stakes scientific communication setting. The faithfulness claims are not substantiated by any measurement (e.g., citation accuracy, quote verification rates, or rates of unmarked fabricated claims).

The benchmark used for main results is very small (top-20 papers, ~100 instances), no statistical significance tests or variance estimates are reported, and the differences (often ~0.3–0.5 on a 0–5 scale) may not be robust.

Baselines are limited to direct-to-text prompting of four LLMs. No comparison with prior rebuttal-writing or argument-alignment systems (e.g., Purkayastha et al. 2023, APE, DISAPE-adjacent work), making the 'first multi-agent framework' claim and the comparative contribution hard to assess.

Human-in-the-loop checkpoints are presented as a core feature ('transparent author response assistance'), but the evaluation is fully automated and includes no user study; the claimed reduction of 'cognitive burden' is unsupported.

Presentation is sloppy and undermines confidence: the title says Paper2Rebuttal while the system is called RebuttalAgent (and the conclusion calls it 'RESPONSEAGENT'); the project page and HF demo links are empty; there are typos (e.g., 'ebuttalAgent', 'Lek'); the filtering paragraph repeats itself verbatim; and the causal claims in Observations 1–3 are over-interpreted from small LLM-judged deltas.

Reproducibility of results is limited: the system and baselines depend on closed-source, versioned commercial APIs, code is only promised, and the benchmark construction pipeline (automatic filtering, ambiguity removal, the 'ranking' for the Challenge set) is described only at a high level.

The evidence-construction module relies on arXiv abstract-level retrieval, yet the rubric rewards 'evidence support' for citing external literature; whether cited evidence is actually accurate and appropriate is never verified, so a claimed core contribution (verifiable grounding) is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored task (rebuttal assistance) with a sensible reframing from free-form generation to decision-and-evidence organization, and the verify-then-write pipeline is clearly motivated.

The system design is well described: concern atomization with coverage checks, concern-conditioned hybrid context, on-demand external evidence, and a plan-checker stage are each concretely specified, and full prompt templates are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the workflow.

A new benchmark (RebuttalBench) derived from real OpenReview ICLR discussion threads with outcome-based positive/negative signals is a useful resource; the ~9.3K corpus plus a focused 100-instance challenge set is a reasonable construction, and the corpus-level statistics are reported.

The experimental design controls the backbone: RebuttalAgent and direct-to-text baselines share the same LLM (GPT-5-mini, Grok-4.1, Gemini-3-Flash, DeepSeekV3.2), so gains are attributable to the structured pipeline rather than model capacity, and consistent improvements across all four backbones support the core claim.

The ablation study isolates each module and yields an interpretable finding (evidence construction as the most critical artifact), and case studies illustrate intermediate artifacts rather than only final prose.
weaknesses: All quantitative results rely on a single LLM-as-judge (Gemini-3-Flash) with a rubric designed by the authors. There is no human evaluation, no validation of judge scores against human judgments, no second judge, and no agreement statistics. The rubric dimensions (coverage, specificity, evidence support) closely mirror the system's design goals, creating a circularity risk: the pipeline may be optimized toward the same rubric used to evaluate it. Length/structure bias of LLM judges toward multi-section, evidence-cited outputs is not controlled for.

The test set is very small (20 papers, ~100 instances in RebuttalBench-Challenge), and no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds/runs are reported; several claimed gains (e.g., +0.06 on some Communication components) are within plausible judge noise.

There is a serious internal inconsistency regarding faithfulness: Section 3.3 claims the system 'explicitly inhibits result generation' and uses TBD placeholders, but the Rebuttal Letter Writer prompt in Appendix D instructs the model to 'invent plausible, realistic values/results' (marked with an asterisk) so the output is not recognizable as AI-written. This directly contradicts the paper's central 'no fabrication / verifiable grounding' claim and raises ethical concerns about the tool's deployment in peer review.

The claimed traceability/verifiability is not actually measured: none of the nine metrics verify that citations are real, that quoted evidence matches the manuscript, or that claims are factually grounded. A dedicated grounding/hallucination metric (e.g., citation validity, claim-entailment checks) would be needed to support the paper's headline claim of 'verifiable grounding.'

The human-in-the-loop component, presented as central to the contribution, is excluded from all main experiments (fully automated mode), so the flagship transparency/control claims are untested; the benchmark also lacks any author-side usability assessment.

Comparisons are limited to direct-to-text prompting with the same backbone; no comparison to prior rebuttal-generation or argumentation methods (e.g., Purkayastha et al. 2023, APE, DISAPERE-based systems), making it hard to situate the contribution against existing work.

Reproducibility is weakened by closed-source models with non-deterministic APIs, an empty project page / HF demo, and code only promised ('will be released'); the judge being the same model family as one backbone raises self-preference concerns that are not addressed.

The paper has notable polish issues: the conclusion names the system 'ResponseAgent' instead of RebuttalAgent; Section 4.1 contains a duplicated sentence; naming is inconsistent (REBUTTALAGENT / RebuttalAgent); and Appendix B says scoring details are in 'Appendix D' while the metric section earlier points to Appendix B, confusing cross-references.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: assisting authors during the rebuttal phase, with an explicit focus on faithfulness, coverage, and verifiability rather than fluency alone. The 'verify-then-write' framing (concern atomization → evidence construction → plan checking → drafting) is a reasonable and clearly motivated decomposition.

The proposed RebuttalBench is built on real ICLR OpenReview interactions with outcome-based (resolved vs. unresolved) labels derived from reviewers' follow-up signals, which is a more meaningful supervision signal than purely subjective quality labels. The data-filtering pipeline and tier-stratification are described in detail, including a human annotation check of the labeling.

The evaluation design is comparatively careful for this line of work: matched-backbone comparisons (same LLM for baseline and agent), ablations of each major module, an additional comparison against RAG, AutoGen, and Ju-Jitsu baselines, a cross-model judge-robustness check, and an author-centric human preference study (9 authors evaluating 33 drafts on their own submissions) with moderate correlation to the automatic metric (Kendall tau = 0.646).

The ablation analysis is honest about a counterintuitive result (checkers slightly lower automated Coverage) and explains it via a qualitative 'coverage paradox' case study, showing awareness of metric-gaming failure modes rather than hiding them.

The discussion of ethical risks (misuse for persuasive-but-unfaithful rebuttals, handling unpublished manuscripts, confidentiality) and the [TBD]-placeholder design for not-yet-run experiments show responsible attention to a sensitive application area.
Prompt templates and rubric anchors are provided in the appendix, which aids reproducibility of the pipeline and the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The core evidence rests on an LLM-as-judge whose rubric (coverage, specificity, evidence support, constructiveness) closely mirrors the design goals of the proposed system. Although the authors provide a human-author correlation study and a judge-swap check, the correlation (tau = 0.646) is moderate, no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported anywhere, and the risk that the pipeline is optimized toward the judge's rubric is not fully dispelled. The paper's own 'coverage paradox' analysis demonstrates that the judge can be gamed, which undermines confidence in absolute score differences of ~0.3–0.5 points.

The evaluation scale is small: the focused benchmark consists of 20 papers / 106 multi-turn cases, and the human study covers 33 samples. Many per-component deltas in Table 1 and Table 2 are small (often < 0.3) and no significance testing is performed, making it difficult to distinguish real gains from judge noise.

Reproducibility is weakened by an empty 'Project Page' and 'HF Demo' field in the manuscript and no released code or data link; the benchmark construction depends on LLM-based filtering and stratification whose exact configurations are hard to reconstruct.

Presentation issues reduce polish and trust: the project-page fields are blank, the ethics statement repeatedly refers to the system as 'AutoRebuttal' (a different name), there are typos ('RebuttalAent', 'INFERENCE'), and the human study references 'CVPR 2026 submissions' evaluated after the rebuttal phase, which is temporally confusing. The human study section also overstates its evidence ('statistically proves', '100.0% accuracy... completely objective and unbiased').

Novelty is moderate: the contribution is primarily an application of known agentic patterns (planner/retriever/checker decomposition, ReAct-style retrieval, LLM verification) to a new domain, plus a domain benchmark. The related-work coverage of rebuttal-generation systems (e.g., Ju-Jitsu, which is only compared in an appendix) and of existing rebuttal datasets (DISAPERE, APE, Re²) suggests the benchmark contribution should be positioned more carefully against prior resources.

Several claimed contributions are not fully delivered in the main evaluation: the human-in-the-loop checkpoints are disabled in all main experiments ('fully automated mode'), so the central claim of transparent, author-controlled assistance is only illustrated via case studies rather than measured; the effect of human feedback on final rebuttal quality is never quantified.

Some reported artifacts are questionable: the gains for the strongest backbones are small and uneven, the '100% annotation accuracy' claim for the automated classifier is based on a very small sample (n=6 Tier-3, n=44 Tier-1), and the appendix baseline comparisons appear only in supplementary material despite being directly relevant to the main claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem: assisting authors during the rebuttal phase, which is a high-stakes, verification-heavy writing task in the NLP/science ecosystem.

The system design is thoughtfully decomposed: concern atomization, manuscript compression with fidelity checking, on-demand external evidence retrieval, plan-level verification before drafting, and optional human-in-the-loop checkpoints. This 'verify-then-write' reframing is a reasonable and defensible design principle.

The evaluation effort is more extensive than typical system papers: four matched backbone LLMs, component ablations (Table 2), additional baselines including RAG, AutoGen, and Jiu-Jitsu (Appendix F), a cross-judge robustness check (Appendix E.1), and an author-centric human preference study with real authors evaluating rebuttals for their own submissions.

The qualitative 'Coverage Paradox' analysis (Sec. 5.3, App. G) is a nice touch, honestly reporting that removing checkers marginally increases the automated coverage score and explaining why, rather than hiding an unfavorable number.
Ethical risks of automated rebuttal assistance are explicitly discussed, including fabrication risks, commitment safety ([TBD] placeholders for unrun experiments), and data policy.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is the central validity concern. RebuttalBench, its 9-component rubric, and the LLM judge were all designed by the authors; the system being evaluated optimizes exactly the properties the rubric rewards (concern coverage, specificity, evidence linkage). There is no evidence the rubric was validated against reviewer behavior or final review outcomes on held-out data. The human study (9 evaluators, 33 samples, Kendall tau = 0.646) helps but is small, and Table 5 shows modest and partially inconsistent human preference differences (e.g., RebuttalAgent-GPT5-mini scoring below the Gemini-3-Flash baseline on some dimensions).

The judge model (Gemini-3-Flash) is also one of the baseline backbones, raising self-preference bias concerns; the GPT-5-mini judge swap mitigates but does not eliminate this, and judge-model agreement is only reported for one swap on one subset.

The benchmark is tiny for its claims: 20 papers and 106 multi-turn cases in the challenge set, drawn from a single venue (ICLR 2023, via the RE^2 dataset). No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, yet differences of 0.3-0.5 points on a 0-5 LLM-judged scale are interpreted as 'consistent', 'significant', and even 'definitive' improvements.

Citation integrity problems undermine trust in the write-up. Several in-text citations do not match the reference list (e.g., 'Lu et al.' cited for peer-review communication maps to 'Efficient diffusion as low light enhancer', a CVPR low-light enhancement paper; 'Team et al., 2023' is cited for Gemini-3-Flash but the reference is the December 2023 Gemini report). Whether careless or LLM-generated, this is disqualifying-level sloppiness for a paper about factual grounding.

Reproducibility is weak: the 'Project Page' and 'HF Demo' fields in the manuscript are empty placeholders, no code or data release is evidenced, and the pipeline depends entirely on closed-source frontier APIs. The benchmark derives from an existing dataset but the filtering/sampling pipeline is only partially specified.

Overclaiming is pervasive: 'the first multi-agent framework' is asserted without justification against closely related rebuttal-generation work (DISAPERE, APE, Re^2, Jiu-Jitsu); phrases like 'statistically proves', 'definitively proves', and 'completely objective and unbiased' appear where the evidence supports no such conclusion (e.g., a 100.0% agreement on 44 labels does not 'definitively prove' ground-truth objectivity).

The manuscript is internally inconsistent and hard to fully trust: futuristic/ambiguous model naming (GPT-5, Gemini-3-Flash, Grok-4.1-fast) with inconsistent access dates, and mixed venue framing (ICLR prompts in the appendix, CVPR 2026 submissions in the human study).

The reported gains are confounded by verbosity and structure: the multi-agent pipeline produces longer, more structured, action-item-formatted responses, which plausibly appeal to a rubric-based LLM judge independent of scientific quality; the paper acknowledges this only for the checker ablation and does not control for response length in the main results.

The human-in-the-loop component, advertised as a core contribution (and central to the safety argument), is disabled in all main experiments, so the actual evaluated system differs from the system described as the contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and under-explored task (LLM-assisted rebuttal writing), and the reframing from direct-to-text generation to a 'verify-then-write' decision-and-evidence organization workflow is a sensible, well-motivated design with clear requirements (coverage, faithfulness, verifiability, global consistency).

The evaluation effort is above average for agent papers: an author-centric human preference study with real authors scoring rebuttals for their own submissions (33 samples, 9 researchers), a Kendall's tau of 0.646 between human and automated scores, a cross-judge robustness check (GPT-5-mini vs. Gemini-3-Flash), and expanded baselines (RAG, AutoGen, Jiu-Jitsu) in the appendix.
Matched-backbone comparisons (RebuttalAgent and baselines sharing the same LLM) isolate the contribution of the pipeline from model capacity, which is methodologically sound.

The ablation study is informative, and the honest analysis of the 'Coverage Paradox' (checkers slightly reduce automated coverage but improve precision/actionability) shows critical self-reflection rather than cherry-picking.

The data filtering pipeline is documented in detail, with a human annotation validation study of the outcome labels and tier stratification, and an ethics/broader-impact statement that acknowledges misuse risks.
Full prompt templates for all agents and the judge are provided, supporting reproducibility of the system design.
weaknesses: Circularity risk in evaluation: RebuttalBench's automated judge is an LLM rubric, and the headline results rest primarily on that judge. The human study is small (33 samples, 9 annotators, CVPR-2026 only), and no statistical significance testing or variance estimates are reported for the main Table 1 gains (0.3–0.6 on a 0–5 scale), so the magnitude and reliability of improvements are hard to verify.
The benchmark test set is very small (20 papers, 106 cases) and drawn from a single venue (ICLR 2023), limiting generalizability claims about 'RebuttalBench' as a broad benchmark.

Serious internal inconsistency with the stated ethics position: the Rebuttal Letter Writer prompt explicitly instructs the model to make output 'not immediately recognizable as an AI-written rebuttal, but should be as close as possible to a real person' and to include 'speculative' experimental data marked with asterisks. This directly conflicts with the paper's transparency claims and its own ethics statement against persuasive/misleading rebuttals, and raises dual-use concerns that the authors do not address.

Numerical inconsistencies between text and tables undermine confidence in the reporting: e.g., Sec. 5.3 states evidence support drops '3.39 to 3.33' and 'rebuttal quality (4.07 to 4.01)' without checkers, but Table 2 shows Evidence Support unchanged (3.39, +0.00) and attributes 4.07→4.01 to Response Engagement; the naming of metrics in the text does not reliably match table columns.

Sloppy presentation: the system name is inconsistent ('RebuttalAgent' vs. 'RebuttalAent' vs. 'AutoRebuttal'), typos persist in figures and case studies ('ablatioins', 'Missing Citatinos'), the Project Page and HF Demo fields are empty, and Appendix H's prompt-template section is largely unpopulated relative to its promise.

The claim of being 'the first multi-agent framework' for rebuttal generation is overstated given the cited prior work (Jiu-Jitsu, multi-agent review systems), and prior rebuttal-generation baselines are evaluated only on the authors' own benchmark with limited tuning, raising fairness questions (e.g., Jiu-Jitsu scoring 1.42 may reflect incompatibility with the pipeline's format rather than method quality).

The human-in-the-loop feature, a central selling point of the system, is entirely absent from quantitative evaluation (all main results are fully automated), so the actual usability claims ('reduces cognitive burden') are supported only anecdotally.
No cost/latency analysis is provided despite the limitations section acknowledging the pipeline's overhead, which matters for assessing practical adoption.
